title: History of Khwajah Hasan al-Habbal
summary: Next stood Khwajah Hasan al-Habbal, the former rope-maker who now resided in an imperial palace.
full_text:
Next stood Khwajah Hasan al-Habbal, the former rope-maker who now resided in an imperial palace.

'O Caliph,' began Hasan, 'two lifelong friends of mine, Sa'ad and Sa'adi, held a perpetual debate. Sa'adi argued that a man becomes wealthy only if given a large sum of gold to trade with. Sa'ad insisted that without divine blessing and industrious labor, gold would slip away like water through fingers, and that modest gifts often build lasting empires.

To test their philosophy, Sa'adi approached me at my modest rope-spinning shed. He pressed two hundred gold dinars into my hands, saying: "Go, buy hemp in bulk and become rich!"

I was overwhelmed. Having never seen such treasure, I tucked ten dinars into my pocket for daily bread and sewed the remaining one hundred and ninety inside the linen fold of my turban. Walking to the market, I stopped at a butcher's stall to buy meat for my hungry children. While negotiating, a ravenous kite smelled the meat, swooped down from the sky, missed the beef, and snatched my turban by its protruding fold! The bird flew across the city walls with all my fortune!

I returned home weeping, poorer and more sorrowful than before.

Six months later, the two friends visited again. Sa'adi, believing I had squandered the gold on follies, shook his head, but gave me another two hundred dinars out of pity.

This time, determined to keep it safe from birds, I hid the gold at the bottom of an earthenware jar filled with wheat bran in my pantry. Days later, while I was out buying hemp, an itinerant merchant came selling washing clay. My wife, knowing nothing of the hidden coins and needing soap clay, traded the old jar of bran for two blocks of soap!

When I returned and found the jar gone, I collapsed in utter despair.

A year passed before Sa'ad and Sa'adi returned. Seeing me still weaving coarse twine in rags, Sa'adi gave up in frustration. But Sa'ad smiled gently. He reached into his robe and handed me a small, worthless piece of lead he had picked up in the street.
"Take this, friend Hasan," said Sa'ad. "It has no market value, but may providence bless it."

I put the scrap of lead on my shelf. That evening, a neighboring fisherman knocked frantically, saying his lead weights had torn away and he needed a sinker immediately to cast his nets before sunset. I gave him my lead scrap. Grateful, he promised: "Whatever comes up in my first net shall be thine!"

The next dawn, the fisherman brought me a large, fine fish. When my wife cleaned it for dinner, she found inside its stomach a brilliant, clear glass pebble. The children played with it as a toy, and at night, it lit the entire room like a lamp!

A Jewish jeweler passing our window noticed the luminescence and offered ten dinars, then a hundred, then ten thousand! It was the celebrated lost diamond of the grand treasury! I sold it for one hundred thousand dinars!

With that fortune, I did not waste or revel; I established great rope manufactories, employed hundreds of honest artisans, and built caravanserais for travelers.

Months later, my workmen discovered a kite's nest in an ancient hollow tree—and inside it was my old turban, the original one hundred and ninety dinars completely intact! Shortly after, a grain merchant returned my old bran jar, having bought it unopened from the soap seller!

Thus did Sa'ad prove his truth: gold given before its appointed season flies away on the wings of kites, but the smallest gift, blessed by honest diligence and heaven's decree, blossoms into enduring abundance.'
moral: Wealth does not come from unearned hoards or careless chance, but from patient industry blessed by providence.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "History of Khwajah Hasan al-Habbal"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
